# brig policy allow

Let a sandbox's program reach a host, and keep the rule for new sandboxes

## Synopsis

```text
brig policy allow [VM] SANDBOX HOST[:PORT] --binary PATH [--access LEVEL] [--save [--to FILE]]
brig policy allow [VM] SANDBOX --draft CHUNK-ID [--rule KEY] [--save [--to FILE]]
```

## Description

Add one network rule to the policy of SANDBOX, as openshell policy update
does, and wait until the sandbox loads it. The rule lets the program --binary
reach HOST on PORT (443 if not given) and no other sandbox gets it.

brig sends the rule to the gateway itself, with annotations that OpenShell
keeps with the policy revision: brig.dev/by=policy-allow, the rule, its host,
port and program, and brig.dev/trace, the run's trace in the activity log.
[`brig audit`](brig-audit.md) shows them as who made the change.

By default the rule inspects HTTP requests and allows the methods that
--access names: read-only (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS), read-write (also POST, PUT,
PATCH) or full. --l4 allows the whole connection instead, without looking at
the requests, and --audit only logs what the access level would deny. The rule
is named allow\_HOST\_PORT, or --rule says how.

brig refuses a wildcard that stands directly above a top-level domain or
another public suffix, such as \*.com, \*.co.uk or \*.github.io, and \* or \*\*. It
asks for --broad before it adds a rule with full access, with --l4, or for a
program path with a wildcard.

With --draft, brig approves the rule that OpenShell drafted from the denials
of the sandbox ([`brig ui`](brig-ui.md) shows them) as it is, with
openshell rule approve. The draft's rule is then the one that --save saves,
so --rule names it.

--save then writes the rule into the sandbox's policy file, so that sandboxes
created from it get the rule too, as [`brig policy save`](brig-policy-save.md) does: it shows the
change to the file first and does not ask. brig checks that it can save
before it changes the sandbox. A sandbox created from the default policy
needs --to NAME, which creates policies/NAME.yaml.

Without VM, the one that [`brig use`](brig-use.md) selected is used.

## Examples

```sh
brig policy allow dev webapp registry.npmjs.org --binary /usr/bin/node
brig policy allow dev webapp api.example.com:8443 --binary /usr/bin/curl --access read-write --save --to webapp
brig policy allow dev webapp --draft ch-17 --rule allow_registry_npmjs_org_443 --save --to webapp
```

## Options

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--access string` | the HTTP methods to allow: read-only, read-write or full (default `read-only`) |
| `--audit` | only log what the access level would deny, and let it pass |
| `--binary string` | the full path of the program that may connect |
| `--broad` | confirm a rule with full access, with --l4, or for a program path with a wildcard |
| `--draft string` | approve OpenShell's draft with this chunk ID, as it is |
| `--l4` | allow the whole connection, without inspecting HTTP requests |
| `--rule string` | the key of the rule (default allow\_HOST\_PORT); with --draft, the draft's rule |
| `--save` | write the rule into the sandbox's policy file, as brig policy save does |
| `--to string` | with --save: save into this policy file, or create policies/NAME.yaml from the sandbox's policy file |
| `-w, --workspace string` | the workspace of the gateway to work in (default: $BRIG\_WORKSPACE, else default) |

The [global options](brig.md#options) of brig apply too.
